chunks: My father, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Muhammad ibn Yahya al-Attar narrated to us, saying: Abu Sa'id al-Adami narrated to us, from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub, from Ali ibn Riyab, from al-Hasan ibn Ziyad al-Attar,

He said: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'They say to us: Are you believers?' So we say: 'Yes, if Allah wills.' They say: 'Are not the believers in Paradise?' We say: 'Yes.' They say: 'So are you in Paradise?' When we look at ourselves, we feel weak and falter in giving an answer.' He (the Imam) said: 'When they say to you: Are you believers?' Say: 'Yes, if Allah wills.' I said: 'And they say: You are excepted only because you are doubtful (shakkak).' He said: 'Say: By Allah, we are not doubtful, but we have used the exception (istithna') as Allah the Exalted said:
You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, if Allah wills, in safety

And He knows that they will enter it first, and Allah the Exalted has named the believers as "believers" based on their good deeds, and He did not name those who committed major sins, regarding whom He promised Hellfire, in the Quran or in tradition as "believers" after that deed.

key_terms.اسْتِثْنَاء: Exception (linguistic/legal device of adding a condition)
key_terms.شُكَّك: Doubtful one (one who is in a state of doubt)

ai.seo_question: Why do Shia Muslims say 'if Allah wills' when claiming to be believers?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Saduq records this dialogue to clarify that the Shia practice of *istithna'* (saying 'if Allah wills') is a humble acknowledgment of divine decree rather than an admission of doubt (*shakk*) regarding one's faith. The Imam cites the Quranic promise of entering the Sacred Mosque to demonstrate that even when the outcome is certain, the exception remains linguistically and theologically valid. Furthermore, he distinguishes between the general title of 'believer' and the specific state of those who commit major sins, noting that scripture does not explicitly label the latter as believers in the same absolute sense.
